extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of poetics / literary criticism and creative writers interested in theoretical criteria for poetry and drama
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotelian criteria for evaluating or composing poetry (epic and tragic), including diction, plausibility, unity, imitation, and the justification of the irrational or impossible in poetic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toleration of absurdity after imparting likelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: “But once it has been framed and an air of likelihood imparted to it, the absurdity itself should be tolerated.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not construct an absurd plot in the first instance; nevertheless, if a poet establishes plausibility or poetic charm (as Homer does in the Odyssey), otherwise intolerable irrational incidents may be accepted. Example: irrational incidents are veiled by poetic charm in Homer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction elaborated in pauses; avoid over-brilliant diction in character/thought
rubrics_metrics.description: “The diction should be elaborated in the pauses of the action, where there is no expression of character or thought. For, conversely, character and thought are merely obscured by a diction that is over brilliant.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve ornate or elaborate language for moments between actions; during direct expression of character or thought, simpler diction is preferable so as not to obscure psychological or ethical detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation: three kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: “The poet being an imitator... must of necessity imitate one of three objects,—things as they were or are, things as they are said or thought to be, or things as they ought to be.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing, decide whether you will base representation on fact, on common belief/tradition, or on idealized/ought-to-be forms; each choice has different justificatory resources and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different standards of correctness across arts
rubrics_metrics.description: “Add to this, that the standard of correctness is not the same in poetry and politics, any more than in poetry and any other art.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetic choices against literary/artistic standards rather than standards proper to other domains (e.g., political or technical correctness); an apparent factual error may be acceptable in poetry under its own criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish essential faults from accidental faults
rubrics_metrics.description: “Within the art of poetry itself there are two kinds of faults—those which touch its essence, and those which are accidental. If a poet has proposed to himself to imitate something, <but has imitated it incorrectly> through want of capacity, the error is inherent in the poetry. But if the failure is due to the thing he has proposed to do... the error is not essential to the poetry.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a flaw undermines the work’s fundamental artistic aims (essential) or is an ancillary mistake (accidental) such as technical inaccuracies in specialized knowledge; essential faults are more damning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify impossibilities by artistic ends; avoid unnecessary violations
rubrics_metrics.description: “First we will suppose the poet has represented things impossible according to the laws of his own art. It is an error; but the error may be justified, if the end of the art be thereby attained... If, however, the end might have been as well, or better, attained without violating the special rules of the poetic art, the error is not justified: for every kind of error should, if possible, be avoided.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce impossible or rule‑breaking elements only when they are necessary to achieve the poem’s proper effect; prefer solutions that respect the art’s rules where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual criteria: consider who, to whom, when, why
rubrics_metrics.description: “In examining whether what has been said or done by some one is poetically right or not, we must not look merely to the particular act or saying, and ask whether it is poetically-good or bad. We must also consider by whom it is said or done, to whom, when, in whose interest, or for what end.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess lines/actions in their dramatic and social context (speaker, audience, timing, motive) rather than in isolation; context can justify otherwise questionable choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve textual/interpretive difficulties via diction and linguistic context
rubrics_metrics.description: “Other difficulties may be resolved by due regard to the diction... We may note a rare word... It may be metaphorical... the solution may depend upon accent or breathing... by punctuation... or by ambiguity of construction... or by the usage of language.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a passage seems problematic, examine vocabulary (dialectal usages, rare words), metaphorical senses, accent/punctuation/orthography, syntactic ambiguity, and customary usages; multiple plausible senses should be weighed rather than faulted hastily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer probable impossibility to improbable possibility; justify irrational by received opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: “The impossible must be justified by reference to artistic requirements, or to the higher reality, or to received opinion. With respect to the requirements of art, a probable impossibility is to be preferred to a thing improbable and yet possible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a choice contradicts reality, justify it either artistically (serves art’s end) or by appeal to common belief/tradition; an idealized impossibility that coheres with artistic aims is better than a weakly plausible but artistically unsatisfying detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrationality and depravity must have inner necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The element of the irrational, and, similarly, depravity of character, are justly censured when there is no inner necessity for introducing them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inserting irrational behavior or morally corrupt characters unless doing so is necessary to the plot, theme, or artistic effect; gratuitous depravity is a legitimate target for criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue of five sources of critical objections
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thus, there are five sources from which critical objections are drawn. Things are censured either as impossible, or irrational, or morally hurtful, or contradictory, or contrary to artistic correctness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending or evaluating a work, anticipate objections in these five categories and prepare answers (e.g., artistic justification, appeal to received opinion, contextualization, linguistic clarification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Match mode to audience refinement; avoid pandering via bad histrionic excess
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the more refined art is the higher, and the more refined in every case is that which appeals to the better sort of audience... Epic poetry is addressed to a cultivated audience, who do not need gesture; Tragedy, to an inferior public. Being then unrefined, it is evidently the lower of the two.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider audience sophistication when choosing mode and presentation. Also note that excessive gesticulation or theatrical extravagance is a defect of performance (histrionic art), not necessarily of the poetic text; avoid pandering to an audience by degrading the poetic means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria favoring Tragedy over Epic
rubrics_metrics.description: “Tragedy... has all the epic elements—it may even use the epic metre—with the music and scenic effects as important accessories; these produce the most vivid of pleasures... the art attains its end within narrower limits; for the concentrated effect is more pleasurable than one which is spread over a long time... Epic imitation has less unity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer forms that deliver concentrated, unified effect with vividness in representation and reading; unity, concentrated magnitude, and the effective use of accessory arts (music, spectacle) are virtues in dramatic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation follows nature but is not literal copying; artists may present the ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: “Art imitates nature... the artist may ‘imitate things as they ought to be’: he may place before him an unrealised ideal. We see at once that there is no question here of bare imitation, of a literal transcript of the world of reality.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic imitation allows idealization: represent types as they ought to be rather than simply copying empirical reality. Use nature as guide to ends and methods but exercise creative idealizing to realize the higher artistic type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification by 'how men say' (received tradition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “If, however, the representation be of neither kind, the poet may answer,—‘This is how men say the thing is.’ This applies to tales about the gods.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a depiction is neither factual nor ideal, it can be defended on the basis of popular belief, tradition, or mythic convention; appeal to received opinion can legitimize departures from fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve apparent contradictions by examining meaning relations and authorial assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: “Things that sound contradictory should be examined by the same rules as in dialectical refutation—whether the same thing is meant, in the same relation, and in the same sense. We should therefore solve the question by reference to what the poet says himself, or to what is tacitly assumed by a person of intelligence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When lines or incidents seem contradictory, analyze whether terms are used in the same sense and relation; prefer interpretations consistent with the poet’s explicit or tacit assumptions before condemning inconsistency.
